name: Embeddings and Vector Search
intent: Turn text or images into vectors where distance means similarity, then find the nearest ones fast by giving up a little exactness.
scenario: A support site stores 10 million help-article chunks as 768-dimension embeddings. A customer asks "refund for a damaged parcel" and the service must return the 10 closest chunks in a few milliseconds, only from that customer's own tenant.
problem: A model can map a sentence to a list of numbers so that sentences with similar meaning land close together. Finding the closest vectors exactly means comparing the query with every stored vector: 10 million distance computations over 3 KB each, about 30 GB read per query. That is far too slow and too big for interactive use, and ordinary database indexes (B-trees, hashes) do not help, because there is no sort order for "nearest" in 768 dimensions.

howItWorks.title: An embedding is a point; distance is meaning
howItWorks.text: An embedding model turns each chunk into a fixed-length vector of floats (a few hundred to a few thousand numbers). Training pushes related inputs close together under a metric: cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance. Query and documents must come from the same model and version, otherwise the distances are meaningless. The vector is a lossy summary of meaning, so "nearest" is only as good as the model.

howItWorks.title: Exact search is a scan, and it does not scale
howItWorks.text: Brute force computes the distance to every vector. At 10 million vectors and 768 dimensions that is about 7.7 billion multiply-adds and 30 GB of memory traffic per query, so even a well-vectorised scan takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds on one machine. It is perfectly fine up to roughly 10^5 to 10^6 vectors, and it is the ground truth you measure approximate indexes against.

howItWorks.title: Approximate indexes skip most of the data
howItWorks.text: IVF clusters the vectors with k-means into nlist cells and keeps one list per cell. A query finds its nprobe nearest centroids and scans only those lists. HNSW instead builds a layered proximity graph: start at the top, greedily hop to closer neighbours, drop a layer, and at the bottom keep a candidate beam of size efSearch. Both examine a tiny fraction of the vectors, and both can miss a true neighbour that sits in a cell or branch they did not visit.

howItWorks.title: Recall, latency and memory are one dial
howItWorks.text: nprobe (IVF) and efSearch (HNSW) set how much you explore. More exploration raises recall@k (the share of the true top k you actually return) and costs more distance computations and latency, with sharply diminishing returns near the top. Graph indexes are fast and recall-rich but keep every vector and link in RAM; IVF builds faster and is smaller. You choose a target recall (often 90 to 99 percent) and then tune the cheapest setting that reaches it on your own data.

howItWorks.title: Compression: product quantisation
howItWorks.text: 768 float32 values are 3,072 bytes per vector, so 10 million vectors are about 30 GB before any index. Product quantisation splits each vector into, say, 96 sub-vectors and replaces each with a one-byte code from a learned codebook: 96 bytes per vector, about 1 GB total, and distances are computed from lookup tables. The price is approximate distances, so systems scan compressed codes and then re-rank the best 100 or so candidates with full-precision vectors, often kept on SSD.

howItWorks.title: Metadata filters and index maintenance
howItWorks.text: Real queries say "only tenant 42" or "published after March". Filtering the results after the ANN search can leave you with fewer than k hits; filtering inside the search (pre-filter, or filter during graph traversal) stays correct but visits more cells or nodes when the filter is selective, and a very selective filter is often better served by an exact scan of the few matching rows. Indexes also cost to build (IVF needs a training pass and retraining as data drifts; HNSW inserts are slower than writes to a plain table) and deletes are usually tombstones cleaned up by a rebuild or compaction.

pros: Finds semantically similar items that keyword matching misses
Search cost grows far slower than the data: a few thousand distance computations out of millions
One knob (nprobe or efSearch) trades recall for latency at query time without a rebuild
Compression makes billion-scale collections fit on a few machines
cons: Results are approximate: a good index still misses some true neighbours, and you must measure how many
Recall depends on the embedding model; a poor model gives confidently wrong neighbours
Memory is large: graph indexes keep vectors and links in RAM
Filtering, updates and deletes are much harder than in a B-tree index
Changing the embedding model means re-embedding and re-indexing everything
whenToUse: Semantic search, recommendations and retrieval for language-model prompts where meaning matters more than exact words
Collections too large for a brute-force scan within the latency budget (roughly above a million vectors)
Deduplication and similarity lookups over images, audio or text
whenNotToUse: Small collections (up to a few hundred thousand vectors): an exact scan is simple, always correct and fast enough
Queries that need exact identifiers, numbers or boolean conditions: use a normal index or full-text search, or combine them with a vector search
Highly selective filters that leave only thousands of candidate rows: filter first and scan them exactly
When you cannot afford to evaluate recall, because an unmeasured ANN index silently drops results
pitfalls: Never measuring recall against a brute-force baseline on real queries, so a wrongly tuned index looks fine until relevant results go missing
Mixing embeddings from different models or versions in one index, or embedding queries with a different model than the documents
Post-filtering by tenant or date after the ANN search, which returns far fewer than k results (or none) for selective filters
Using the wrong metric: vectors that are not normalised with an inner-product index, or cosine in one place and Euclidean in another
Tuning on average latency only: high nprobe or efSearch on a few queries creates a long tail, so watch p99
Forgetting that deletes and updates leave tombstones and stale graph links, so recall and memory degrade until the index is rebuilt
Training IVF centroids on a sample that does not resemble production data, which gives lopsided cells where one list holds a large share of all vectors

roles.label: Search service
roles.description: Receives the customer's question, applies the tenant filter and returns the results.

roles.label: Embedding model
roles.description: Maps the query text to a 768-dimension vector using the same model that embedded the documents.

roles.label: ANN index
roles.description: IVF cells or an HNSW graph; chooses which vectors are worth comparing.

roles.label: Vector store
roles.description: Holds compressed codes in memory and full-precision vectors on SSD for re-ranking.
